items.followUp: What is the halogen family called in the periodic table? Give two examples.

rubric.why: Identifies the group to which halogens belong.
rubric.description: States that halogens are the Group 17 elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying Group 17 (or VIIA).

rubric.why: Provides one correct halogen example.
rubric.description: Names any one halogen as an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: Halogens are the reactive non-metal elements of Group 17 (VIIA) of the periodic table.
Example: chlorine (Cl).

items.followUp: What is the difference between a dilute and a concentrated solution?

rubric.why: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a specified temperature.
rubric.description: Defines a saturated solution by its maximum solute content.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it contains the maximum amount of solute at that temperature.

rubric.why: An unsaturated solution contains less than the maximum amount and can dissolve more solute at that temperature.
rubric.description: Defines an unsaturated solution in contrast to a saturated one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it can dissolve more solute or contains less than the maximum amount.

modelAnswer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a particular temperature.
An unsaturated solution contains less than this maximum amount, so more solute can still dissolve at that temperature.

items.followUp: Calculate the mass/mass percentage of a solution containing 8 g of solute in 200 g of solution.

accept: mass of solute / mass of solution
mass of solute ÷ mass of solution
mass of solute / total mass of solution
rubric.why: The percentage is calculated using the mass of solute divided by the total mass of solution.
rubric.description: Gives the mass/mass percentage relationship.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct ratio of solute mass to solution mass.

rubric.why: Multiplying the mass ratio by 100 expresses it as a percentage; the example illustrates this correctly.
rubric.description: Includes the percentage conversion and a suitable example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for multiplying by 100 and giving a correct example, such as 10 g solute in 100 g solution = 10% m/m.

modelAnswer: Percentage mass/mass (m/m) = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100%.
For example, 10 g of salt in 100 g of solution gives (10 g ÷ 100 g) × 100% = 10% m/m.

items.followUp: Name the three isotopes of hydrogen and state how deuterium can be used to release energy.

rubric.why: Protium is one of the three hydrogen isotopes.
rubric.description: Names protium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying protium (hydrogen-1).

rubric.why: Deuterium is one of the three hydrogen isotopes.
rubric.description: Names deuterium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying deuterium (hydrogen-2).

rubric.why: Tritium is the third hydrogen isotope.
rubric.description: Names tritium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying tritium (hydrogen-3).

rubric.why: In fusion, hydrogen isotopes such as deuterium and tritium combine to form helium.
rubric.description: Explains that energy generation uses fusion of hydrogen isotopes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing fusion of hydrogen isotopes to form helium.

rubric.why: The fusion reaction releases energy, which can be used to generate electricity.
rubric.description: States the energy output or its use in power generation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the released energy is used to generate power or electricity.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium (¹H), deuterium (²H) and tritium (³H).
In power generation, deuterium and tritium nuclei can undergo nuclear fusion.
They combine to form a helium nucleus and a neutron, releasing a large amount of energy.
This energy can be used to generate electricity.

items.followUp: Explain the formation of a coordinate covalent bond in the hydronium ion, H₃O⁺.

rubric.why: A coordinate covalent bond involves a shared pair of electrons.
rubric.description: Defines the bond as a shared electron pair.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a pair of electrons is shared.

rubric.why: Unlike an ordinary covalent bond, both electrons in the shared pair come from one atom.
rubric.description: States that the shared pair is donated by one atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for making clear that one atom supplies both bonding electrons.

rubric.why: The donating atom supplies the pair from one of its lone pairs.
rubric.description: Identifies the donated pair as a lone pair.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning a lone pair on the donor atom.

rubric.why: Ammonia donates its lone pair to H⁺ to form NH₄⁺, a standard example.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of coordinate bond formation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the formation of NH₄⁺ from NH₃ and H⁺.

rubric.why: In NH₄⁺, nitrogen is the donor and the bond can be represented by an arrow from N to H.
rubric.description: Identifies the donor or shows the direction of donation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying nitrogen as the donor or correctly showing the bond's direction.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is donated by one atom.
The donor atom must have a lone pair, and the other atom or ion must be able to accept it.
For example, nitrogen in NH₃ donates its lone pair to H⁺ to form NH₄⁺.
The bond may be shown by an arrow from the donor nitrogen to hydrogen: N→H.

items.followUp: Define vapour pressure and state how increasing temperature affects it.

rubric.why: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by vapour in equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container at a given temperature.
rubric.description: Defines vapour pressure and includes equilibrium with the liquid.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a definition identifying the vapour's pressure and its equilibrium with the liquid; award 1 mark if only the pressure of the vapour is stated.

rubric.why: Temperature affects vapour pressure; increasing temperature increases it.
rubric.description: Identifies temperature as a factor and states its effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that vapour pressure increases as temperature increases.

rubric.why: The nature of the liquid, including the strength of its intermolecular forces, affects its vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Identifies the nature or volatility of the liquid as another factor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the nature of the liquid, volatility, or intermolecular forces.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapour of a liquid when the vapour and liquid are in equilibrium in a closed container at a given temperature.
It depends on the temperature and the nature of the liquid (or the strength of its intermolecular forces).
An increase in temperature increases vapour pressure; a more volatile liquid generally has a higher vapour pressure.

items.followUp: What are metals? State three of their physical properties.

rubric.why: Non-metals are elements that generally lack the characteristic physical properties of metals.
rubric.description: Defines non-metals as elements with non-metallic characteristics.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as elements that are not metals or generally lack metallic properties.

rubric.why: Non-metals are generally poor conductors of heat and electricity.
rubric.description: States their poor electrical or thermal conductivity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct conductivity property.

rubric.why: Solid non-metals generally lack metallic lustre.
rubric.description: States that non-metals are generally dull.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for lack of lustre.

rubric.why: Solid non-metals are generally brittle and cannot be drawn into wires or hammered into sheets.
rubric.description: States brittleness or lack of malleability/ductility.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct mechanical property.

modelAnswer: Non-metals are elements that do not show the characteristic physical properties of metals.
They are generally poor conductors of heat and electricity.
They are generally dull, or non-lustrous.
When solid, they are usually brittle and are neither malleable nor ductile.

items.followUp: Define relative molecular mass and state whether it has a unit.

rubric.why: Relative atomic mass compares an element's average atomic mass with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
rubric.description: Defines relative atomic mass using the carbon-12 standard.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the comparison with 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom's mass.

rubric.why: As a ratio, relative atomic mass has no unit; atomic mass values are also commonly expressed in atomic mass units.
rubric.description: States the unit convention for relative atomic mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is dimensionless/no unit. Also accept amu or u if following the textbook's stated convention.

modelAnswer: Relative atomic mass (Aᵣ) is the average mass of an atom of an element compared with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
It is a ratio, so it has no unit (atomic masses are often expressed in atomic mass units, u).
